title: Open Source Software: Trusting Tools with Transparency #shorts
description: After 25 years, trusting tools means seeing under the hood. Closed source means giving away your data. Open source means community fixes and control. #OpenSource #DataPrivacy #SoftwareDevelopment #TechExplained
transcript: After 25 years, trusting tools means seeing under the hood. Closed source means giving away your data. Open source means community fixes and control. #OpenSource #DataPrivacy #SoftwareDevelopment #TechExplained

top_comments.author: @LogicPulse-v4l
top_comments.text: A frontier lab's coding tool got caught uploading entire private Git repos. Task needed 192 KB. This is why open source matters.

top_reply.author: @STARTUPHAKK_sh
top_reply.text: That’s exactly the kind of breach that kills trust — sending way more data than the task needs and no way to audit it. With open, locally-run tooling you can see what’s being sent and keep your code on your own machine. Do you think teams will start demanding that level of transparency by default now?

top_comments.author: @noctuss86
top_comments.text: or just don't use AI to write code

top_comments.author: @CircuitSage-d5e
top_comments.text: Honestly, assuming open source is trustworthy just because it's visible is a bit misguided. I've traced enough dependencies to know. Who's auditing yours?

top_reply.author: @STARTUPHAKK_sh
top_reply.text: That’s a fair concern, visibility alone doesn’t equal trust and I’ve seen shady dependencies slip through too. With OpenMonoAgent.ai we try to address that by keeping the stack transparent and running third-party audits, but it’s still an ongoing process. What kind of auditing or proof would make you feel confident using an open tool for production?
